metaDescription: What Ontario homeowners should know before hiring a retaining wall contractor, including the permit and engineering rule for walls over 1 metre.
intro: A retaining wall is holding back soil under load, so drainage and engineering matter more here than in almost any other exterior project. In Ontario, walls over roughly 1 metre, about 3.3 feet, typically require a building permit and often engineered drawings, and a contractor who is not fluent in that rule is a warning sign on its own.
whatToLookFor: Clear understanding of when a wall over 1 metre needs a permit and engineering
Experience with segmental block, natural stone and poured concrete systems
A defined drainage plan, including gravel backfill and weeping tile behind the wall
Proper base compaction and setback from property lines or structures
Photos of walls at least a couple of years old to check for bulging or settling
typicalCostNotes: Cost is driven mainly by wall height, length, material and how much excavation and drainage work is involved, so a low garden wall in segmental block generally costs far less per foot than a tall engineered wall in natural stone. Taller walls also carry engineering and permit fees on top of construction, so ask whether those are included in a quote or billed separately.
questionsToAsk: Does this wall's height trigger a permit or engineering requirement here?
What is the drainage plan, and will there be weeping tile behind the wall?
How is the base prepared and compacted before the first course goes in?
Who is the engineer of record if drawings are required, and are they included in price?
What is the warranty on workmanship for settling or bulging after installation?
redFlags: Proposes a wall over 1 metre with no mention of a permit or engineer
No drainage or weeping tile plan behind the wall
Skips base compaction or shortens the buried base course to save time
